items.title: Show HN: Concord – let Claude Code, Codex and Cursor talk to each other
items.why_it_matters: Concord is an MCP and CLI tool that lets different coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor communicate with each other so they don't overwrite each other's work or duplicate tasks. Since you use both Claude Code and Codex, this solves the coordination problem when you have multiple sessions running. You can try installing Concord via npm this week and linking your Claude Code and Codex environments to keep your AI-ingest workspace in sync.

items.title: Show HN: I built a site to share and find Claude Code passes
items.why_it_matters: Claude Coupons is a community-built exchange site where paid Claude users share their referral passes to earn free usage credits. When someone redeems your coupon, Anthropic credits you $10, helping you offset your tool costs. You can try running `/passes` in your Claude Code terminal today, grab your coupon codes, and list them on the site to start racking up free building credits.

items.title: Show HN: My Claude quota ran out in 10 minutes, so I made a tool to find out why
items.why_it_matters: Tare is a lightweight utility designed to analyze your Claude API and Claude Code usage to show you exactly why and where your token quota is draining. It helps prevent unexpected lockouts by highlighting heavy context files that are eating up your limits. You can try running Tare against your AI-ingest project directory this week to see which files are bloating your Claude Code prompts.

items.title: I Cut 80%+ of Context Overhead in My Coding Agent
items.why_it_matters: An indie developer shared how they cut context overhead in their coding agent by over 80% using dynamic tool selection instead of dumping entire files into the prompt. This directly reduces token costs and speeds up response times when you are vibe coding. You can try reviewing your current Claude Code system prompts this week and explicitly telling the agent to read only the specific Next.js components it needs rather than the entire directory.

items.title: Show HN: Watches user sessions, finds bugs that matter, and fixes them
items.why_it_matters: Opslane is an open-source agent that monitors user sessions, identifies bugs, and automatically submits GitHub pull requests with verified fixes. This is a great fit for your Next.js and Supabase stack to catch silent frontend errors without you having to manually debug. You can try linking Opslane to your AI-ingest GitHub repository this week to let it automatically scan for and draft PRs for any bugs in your code.

items.title: Show HN: Proval – Self-hosted code review agent for GitLab, Forgejo, and GitHub
items.why_it_matters: Proval is a self-hosted code review agent for GitHub that automatically reviews your commits and pull requests. As you build up your Git discipline on the AI-ingest repo, this gives you an automated second pair of eyes to verify the code your AI tools are writing before you merge. You can try setting up Proval as a GitHub Action on your repository this week to review your next feature branch.

items.title: Show HN: Scheduled Claude Code agents that cost nothing on a quiet day
items.why_it_matters: Shadok is a tool that lets you schedule Claude Code agents to run automated tasks on a cron schedule while keeping costs at zero when there is no work to do. This is highly useful for automating background tasks like running tests or checking for API updates. You can try setting up a basic scheduled agent this week to run a daily health check on your Next.js and Supabase backend.
